### 01 · Choosing a meter
Group: **Checking your glucose** · Referral chip: **Ask a pharmacist CDE** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `meters` — OneTouch Verio Reflect Meter (4287), Contour NEXT ONE Meter (4524), Accu-Chek Guide Meter (4556), FreeStyle Lite Meter (4402)

- A meter reads a drop of blood from a finger prick. The drop goes on a test strip, and the strip goes into the meter `1.1`
- You can get a meter at most pharmacies, or from your diabetes educator `1.2`
- Once you have a meter, get trained on it before you start using it `1.3`
- How often you check depends on your treatment plan. Your team will tell you when, and how often `1.4`
- Even if you use a sensor, Diabetes Canada suggests keeping a meter and strips, to double-check a reading and as a backup `1.5`

> **Note** `1.note` — Ask your pharmacist or educator which meter suits you. Coverage is under How supplies get paid for, below.

*Sources for this card:* Checking Blood Sugar (Diabetes Canada); Technology & Devices (Diabetes Canada)

### 02 · Strips, lancets and control solution that match
Group: **Checking your glucose** · Referral chip: **Ask a pharmacist CDE** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `matching` — `oneTouch`: OneTouch Verio Test Strips (4948), OneTouch Delica Plus 33G (4458), One Touch Ultra Control Solution (7356); `contour`: Contour Next Test Strips (4714), Bayer Microlet Lancets 28G (4398); `accuChek`: Accu-Chek Guide Test Strips (4656), Accu-Chek Softclix (4945); `freeStyle`: FreeStyle Lite Test Strips (4698), FreeStyle Lancets (4872), FreeStyle Control Solution (4663)

- Diabetes Canada suggests asking which test strips to use with your meter, and whether your meter needs to be coded to read them `2.1`
- Used lancets go in a sharps container. Many pharmacies give out puncture-proof containers and swap a full one for a new one `2.2`
- In Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, the Health Products Stewardship Association (HPSA) gives out free sharps containers at participating collection locations, such as pharmacies `2.3`
- HPSA says never to put sharps in the garbage or the recycling `2.4`
- Elsewhere in Canada, ask your pharmacy how to return used sharps `2.5`

> **Note** `2.note` — If you’re not sure a strip, lancet or control solution fits your meter, check your meter’s guide or ask your pharmacist before you use it.

*Sources for this card:* Checking Blood Sugar (Diabetes Canada); Technology & Devices (Diabetes Canada); Getting Started with Insulin (Diabetes Canada); Returning Medical Sharps (Health Products Stewardship Association)

### 04 · Sensors: which pairs with what
Group: **Checking your glucose** · Referral chip: **Ask a pharmacist CDE** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `readers` — FreeStyle Libre 3 Reader (4674), Dexcom G7 Receiver (4723)

- A sensor sits on your skin like a small patch, held on by adhesive, with a thin filament just under the skin. It measures sugar in the fluid between your cells, so it can read your sugar without a finger prick each time `4.1`
- Some sensors give a reading only when you scan them with your phone. Others show your sugar all the time and can sound alarms for lows and highs `4.2`
- Some sensors connect to an insulin pump. That connection is what a hybrid closed-loop system needs `4.3`
- Diabetes Canada says this technology isn’t for everyone, and suggests talking with your team about whether it’s right for you `4.4`

> **Note** `4.note` — Makers update which devices work together. Before you switch a sensor or a pump, check with your team, your device maker or a Liivv pharmacist who is a Certified Diabetes Educator (CDE).

*Sources for this card:* Technology & Devices (Diabetes Canada); Checking Blood Sugar (Diabetes Canada)

### 05 · Wearing a sensor, and time in range
Group: **Checking your glucose** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `wearing` — Libre Oval Patch (4841), Dexcom G7 Design Patches (Pack of 1) (4310)

- Time in range is the share of your day that your sugar stays in your target range `5.1`
- For most people, Diabetes Canada’s guideline aims for more than 70% of the day between 3.9 and 10.0 mmol/L `5.2`
- It also aims for less than 4% of the day below 3.9 `5.3`
- Breakthrough T1D says going from 60% to 65% of the day in range adds about an hour a day in range `5.4`
- Targets can be different in pregnancy, and for children, older adults and people who have lows often. Your team sets yours `5.5`
- You can share your sensor readings from your phone with your diabetes team, so they can see your patterns over time `5.6`
- A sensor and a finger check are more likely to differ when you’re eating or exercising. If how you feel doesn’t match your sensor, or you’re treating a low, a finger check gives the most accurate number `5.7`

> **Note** `5.note` — Some Diabetes Canada pages give the range as 4.0 to 10.0. If your team gave you a range, use theirs. *(kept outside the collapsed part of the card)*

*Sources for this card:* Checking Blood Sugar (Diabetes Canada); Blood Glucose Monitoring in Adults and Children with Diabetes: Update 2021 (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Time in Range (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF)); Technology & Devices (Diabetes Canada)

### 06 · Sensor restock calculator
Group: **Checking your glucose** · Referral chip: **Ask a pharmacist CDE** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `restock` — Dexcom G7 Sensor 1-Pack (4227), FreeStyle Libre 3 Plus Sensor (4316), FreeStyle Libre 2 Sensor (4479), Guardian 4 Sensor (pk of 5) (4967)

- Your sensor’s guide says how many days each sensor is worn. The calculator multiplies that by the number of sensors you have `6.1`
- If a program pays for your sensors, it may limit how many you get. For example, for one sensor it covers, the Non-Insured Health Benefits (NIHB) program for eligible First Nations and Inuit allows up to 14 every 6 months, with prior approval, for people who manage their diabetes with insulin `6.2`
- Your province or territory may set its own limits. Ask your pharmacist, or see How supplies get paid for, below `6.3`

> **Note** `6.note` — The calculator does arithmetic only. It doesn’t know your coverage, and it can’t count a sensor that stops early.

*Sources for this card:* Non-Insured Health Benefits program updates (Indigenous Services Canada (Non-Insured Health Benefits))

### 07 · Pen needles: length and angle
Group: **Getting insulin in** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes educator** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `penNeedles` — Nano PRO Pen Needles 4mm 32G (4777), EZH Oracle 32g 4mm Pen Needle (7544), Ultra-Fine Pen Needles 5mm 31G (4342)

- An insulin pen comes filled with insulin. You put a new needle tip on for each injection `7.1`
- You need a separate pen for each type of insulin you use `7.2`
- Diabetes Canada suggests shorter, thinner needles. Diabète Québec suggests 4, 5 or 6 mm, so the insulin doesn’t go into muscle `7.3`
- For adults, Diabète Québec says a skin lift may not be needed with a 4 mm needle, and to use one with a needle 8 mm or longer `7.4`
- Diabetes Canada says to put the needle in at 90°, with a quick, smooth motion. With a longer needle, 8 or 12 mm, you may need to gently lift the skin, or go in at 45° `7.5`
- If there’s little fat on your arms, legs or belly, Diabète Québec says a skin lift may be needed even with a 5 or 6 mm needle `7.6`

> **Note** `7.note` — Your educator or pharmacist can show you which length suits you, and how to lift the skin if you need to.

*Sources for this card:* Technology & Devices (Diabetes Canada); Getting Started with Insulin (Diabetes Canada); All about injections (Diabète Québec)

### 08 · Syringes, and insulin strength
Group: **Getting insulin in** · Referral chip: **Ask a pharmacist** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `syringes` — Ultra-Fine Insulin Syringes 0.3mL (4655), Ultra-Fine Insulin Syringes 0.5mL (4467), Ultra-Fine Insulin Syringes 1mL (4474)

- Today’s syringes are smaller and use thinner needles. They cost less than pens and pumps `8.1`
- Insulin comes in more than one strength. Most is U-100 (100 units/mL). Some insulins are stronger, such as U-200, U-300, U-500 or U-700, and each of these comes in its own pen `8.2`
- If you use a pump, Diabetes Canada suggests keeping rapid-acting insulin pens or syringes as a backup `8.3`
- Flying? The Canadian Air Transport Security Authority (CATSA) says a syringe needs its needle guard on, and the insulin it’s for has to be with you `8.4`
- If your insulin is stronger than U-100 (the label says 200, 300, 500 or 700 units/mL), never use a syringe to take it out of the pen. A syringe can’t measure it correctly, and you could get far too much insulin and a severe low `8.5`

> **Note** `8.note` — Always carry a spare pen and needles. If your pen stops working, or you can’t use it, ask your pharmacist what to do before you use a syringe. *(kept outside the collapsed part of the card)*

*Sources for this card:* Technology & Devices (Diabetes Canada); Getting Started with Insulin (Diabetes Canada); Diabetic supplies (Canadian Air Transport Security Authority); Product Monograph Including Patient Medication Information: TOUJEO SoloSTAR, TOUJEO DoubleSTAR (sanofi-aventis Canada Inc. / Health Canada Drug Product Database); Product Monograph: HUMALOG, HUMALOG 200 units/mL KwikPen, HUMALOG MIX25, HUMALOG MIX50 (Eli Lilly Canada Inc. / Health Canada Drug Product Database); Product Monograph Including Patient Medication Information: TRESIBA (Novo Nordisk Canada Inc. / Health Canada Drug Product Database); Product Monograph Including Patient Medication Information: AWIQLI (Novo Nordisk Canada Inc. / Health Canada Drug Product Database); Product Monograph Including Patient Medication Information: ENTUZITY KwikPen (Eli Lilly Canada Inc. / Health Canada Drug Product Database); Humalog (insulin lispro) KwikPen 200 Units/mL - Information on Correct Use to Minimize Medication Errors (Health Canada, Recalls and safety alerts (archived)); Dose Confusion When Switching between Insulin Delivery Devices (ISMP Canada (Institute for Safe Medication Practices Canada))

### 09 · Giving an injection, step by step
Group: **Getting insulin in** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes educator** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `sharps` — Sharps Container 1L (4350)

**Before you start** `9.s1`

- Wash your hands with soap and water, and make sure the injection site is clean `9.s1.1`
- You don’t need to wipe your skin with alcohol. If you do, let it dry completely first `9.s1.2`
- Check the expiry date on your cartridge or vial `9.s1.3`
- Wipe the rubber seal on the pen or vial with alcohol before you put on a new needle. Don’t wipe the needle itself `9.s1.4`
- Cloudy insulin needs mixing until it looks milky white: roll it 10 times between your hands, then tip it upside down and back 10 times. Don’t shake it `9.s1.5`

**The injection** `9.s2`

- Put on a new needle, then prime the pen to check the needle isn’t blocked, the way your pen’s instructions say `9.s2.1`
- Dial the dose your team has set `9.s2.2`
- Put the needle in at 90° with a quick, smooth motion `9.s2.3`
- Press the button until the counter shows 0, or the syringe is empty. Count to 10 before you take the needle out `9.s2.4`
- Put the needle straight into your sharps container. Don’t leave a needle on your pen between injections `9.s2.5`
- Don’t inject through clothing `9.s2.6`

> **Note** `9.note` — Your pen comes with an instruction book. Diabetes Canada suggests reading it, so you know how your pen works.

*Sources for this card:* Getting Started with Insulin (Diabetes Canada); All about injections (Diabète Québec)

### 10 · Choosing and moving your sites
Group: **Getting insulin in** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes educator** · Products shown: *none*

- Change where you inject each time. Diabetes Canada says this helps prevent fatty lumps that can make insulin work poorly `10.1`
- Insulin goes in fastest and most evenly from the belly. Stay about 5 cm (2 inches), three finger widths, from your belly button `10.2`
- Insulin goes in more slowly from the buttocks and thighs. The back of the upper arm is hard to reach on your own, so it’s often not suggested `10.3`
- Diabète Québec suggests leaving at least 1 to 2 cm, about a finger width, between injections, and splitting each area into four zones, using one zone for a week before you move on `10.4`
- Check and feel your injection areas regularly for lumps or dents `10.5`
- Avoid scars, moles and any other changes in the skin `10.6`
- Diabète Québec says injecting into a part of your body you’re about to exercise can make insulin act faster and lower your sugar `10.7`

> **Note** `10.note` — If you find a lump or a dent, show it to your educator or your team.

*Sources for this card:* Getting Started with Insulin (Diabetes Canada); All about injections (Diabète Québec)

### 11 · Keeping insulin safe
Group: **Getting insulin in** · Referral chip: **Ask a pharmacist** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `keepCool` — Frio Insulin Cooling Wallet Small (4844), Frio Individual Insulin Cooling Wallets (4812), Frio Insulin Cooling Wallet Duo (4799)

- Diabète Québec says to keep unopened insulin in the fridge, at 2 to 8 °C `11.1`
- Keep the insulin you’re using at room temperature `11.2`
- Throw out insulin that has frozen, been above 30 °C, or expired `11.3`
- How long an opened pen or vial lasts depends on the product. Diabète Québec says most are good for up to 28 days once opened, and some for longer. Follow the leaflet that came with your insulin `11.4`
- Check the expiry date before you open a new cartridge or vial `11.5`
- Diabetes Canada says insulin goes in your carry-on when you fly, not in checked luggage `11.6`
- CATSA lets insulin, juice and gels through security above the 100 mL limit, but you need to declare them separately `11.7`

*Sources for this card:* All about injections (Diabète Québec); Getting Started with Insulin (Diabetes Canada); Air Travel (Diabetes Canada); Diabetic supplies (Canadian Air Transport Security Authority)

### 12 · Pumps and automated insulin delivery, in plain words
Group: **Getting insulin in** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown: *none*

- An insulin pump is a small device worn outside your body. It gives insulin through a small tube under the skin, 24 hours a day `12.1`
- It gives a small, steady trickle of insulin between meals and overnight. Extra doses can be given when they’re needed, for food or to bring a high down `12.2`
- Some pumps connect to a sensor and respond to your readings. Diabetes Canada calls this a hybrid closed-loop system. You may also hear it called automated insulin delivery `12.3`
- For type 1 diabetes, Diabetes Canada’s guideline prefers automated insulin delivery for everyone who is willing and able to wear and use the devices `12.4`
- Your team works with you to decide whether a pump suits you, and on your pump settings `12.5`

> **Note** `12.note` — Help with paying for a pump depends on where you live. See How supplies get paid for, below.

*Sources for this card:* Technology & Devices (Diabetes Canada); Glycemic Management Across the Lifespan for People With Type 1 Diabetes (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines)

### 14 · Pump backup and set changes
Group: **Getting insulin in** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `pumpBackup` — IV 3000 Infusion Set Dressing (4532), MiniMed Disposable Power Kit (4823), Ultra-Fine Insulin Syringes 1mL (4474)

- Diabetes Canada suggests making a pump backup plan before you need one `14.1`
- Backup supplies include rapid-acting insulin pens or syringes, long-acting insulin if your team says you need it, extra infusion sets and reservoirs, and ketone strips or a blood ketone meter `14.2`
- Learn how to switch to injections in case you can’t use your pump, and keep a written copy of your pump settings `14.3`
- Used infusion sets and sensor applicators with needles go in a sharps container. HPSA’s program takes them in Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. Elsewhere, ask your pharmacy `14.4`

> **Note** `14.note` — How often to change your set, and where to put it, are part of your pump training. If your sugar is high and you can’t explain it, check your ketones and follow On a pump: an unexplained high, in Staying Safe. *(kept outside the collapsed part of the card)*

*Sources for this card:* Technology & Devices (Diabetes Canada); Managing Diabetes in Emergency Situations (Diabetes Canada); Returning Medical Sharps (Health Products Stewardship Association); Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and ketones (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF))

*Sources for the band:* Comparisons by Province/Territory (Diabetes Canada); Non-Insured Health Benefits program updates (Indigenous Services Canada (Non-Insured Health Benefits)); Life-sustaining therapy (Canada Revenue Agency); Disability-Related Information 2025 (RC4064) (Canada Revenue Agency)

**How supplies get paid for** `band.heading`

- **It depends where you live** `band.1` — Coverage for pumps, sensors, test strips and needles is different in each province and territory. Diabetes Canada compares them side by side.
  - **Comparisons by Province/Territory — Diabetes Canada** `band.1.link.1`  
    <https://www.diabetes.ca/advocacy-and-policy/advocacy-reports/comparisons-by-province-territory> · same tab, an English page · shown on /en and /fr  
    *Register:* Comparisons by Province/Territory (Diabetes Canada)
- **First Nations and Inuit (NIHB)** `band.2` — For eligible First Nations and Inuit, the Non-Insured Health Benefits (NIHB) program covers some sensors for people who manage their diabetes with insulin. Some need prior approval. It also covers up to 800 test strips every 100 days for people who use insulin.
  - **Non-Insured Health Benefits program updates — Indigenous Services Canada** `band.2.link.1`  
    <https://www.sac-isc.gc.ca/eng/1578079214611/1578079236012> · same tab, an English page · shown on /en and /fr  
    *Register:* Non-Insured Health Benefits program updates (Indigenous Services Canada (Non-Insured Health Benefits))
- **The disability tax credit** `band.3` — The Canada Revenue Agency treats type 1 diabetes as meeting its life-sustaining therapy test. You still need to apply, with form T2201 or online.
  - **Disability tax credit: life-sustaining therapy — Canada Revenue Agency** `band.3.link.1`  
    <https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/individuals/segments/tax-credits-deductions-persons-disabilities/disability-tax-credit/eligible-dtc/life-sustaining-therapy.html> · same tab, an English page · shown on /en and /fr  
    *Register:* Life-sustaining therapy (Canada Revenue Agency)

**Tools you know well** `closing.heading`

This is general information, not medical advice, and it is not a substitute for care from your diabetes team, doctor or pharmacist. Your treatment, your devices and your settings depend on you. Your team sets them. Device details come from each maker’s Canadian site, or a government program, on the date shown, and can change. `disclaimer`

## Questions for the nurse

*Where the Canadian sources disagree, or a line needed a clinical judgement, the copy above uses a default. None of these is settled: each line named under "Where" renders the default today, in both locales. Rule on each one — keep the default, or take the alternative — and the copy is changed to match. Reviewer-only: none of this renders on a page.*

- **R16.** Default used: **URGENT (owner and nurse). Picker facts that rest only on makers’ pages.** Policy 4 says an industry page is never the only source, but wear times, pairings and box contents are mostly on makers’ pages. Default: the pickers show each fact with its basis line, its sources and the date checked. The bases after the source check and ruling C42 (2026-10-06): `twoMakers` (G7 and G6 with Omnipod 5; G6 with mylife Loop; G7 with the t:slim X2, still with Dexcom’s "not all connections are available in Canada"; the G6 → G7 notice), `government` (Guardian 4 with the 780G, from NIHB), `pumpMakerOnly` (Libre 3 Plus with mylife Loop; G6 with the t:slim X2, from Tandem’s Canadian user guide). No pairing is `sensorMakerOnly` now. Maker-only facts: the G7 and Libre 3 Plus wear times, the Libre 3 Plus recall notice, every fact line in the pump picker, and the held meter picker. Brand names appear only in the pickers and the calculator’s presets (`device-pairings.ts`).  
  *Where:* `2.fig`, `4.fig`, `6.fig`, `13.fig`  
  *Alternative:* (a) Show only `government` and `twoMakers` entries. (b) Also hold the `pumpMakerOnly` and `sensorMakerOnly` entries and every maker-only fact line (a `makerOnlyFacts` hold). (c) Hold all the pickers until a Canadian non-industry page (for example Health Canada’s Medical Devices Active Licence Listing, not registered) confirms each fact.

**Before publishing — factual checks, not clinical rulings:**

1. Done by the source check: the four pages it could not read word for word at first were saved and re-read, and every claim on them is confirmed. Their facts, and the locator corrections the check listed (`dc-getting-started-with-insulin` names no 6 mm needle; `dexcom-g7-wear-time` says "up to 10 days" and nothing on restarts; `minimed-canada` no longer names Guardian 4; `dexcom-pumps-and-pens` names only G7 for the t:slim X2, with its Canada footnote), are now in `sources-review.ts`.
2. Libre 3 Plus recall notice (the sensor picker, under Libre 3 Plus in the pump picker’s lists, and under its calculator preset; one notice in `device-pairings.ts`, marked `everywhere`): re-check Abbott’s Canadian site on publish day, and drop the notice from `device-pairings.ts` if it is gone.
3. Dexcom’s "Pumps and pens" page is out of date on where Omnipod 5 is available (its footnote says Ontario and Nova Scotia only). Only its pairings are used; re-check them.
4. Omnipod’s Canadian page mixes in blocks from other countries (a UK 0800 number, Libre 2 Plus). Re-check whether Insulet Canada now lists a Libre sensor for Canada.
5. Tandem: re-confirm Control-IQ+ from age 2, "Dexcom CGM sold separately" and the four-year limited warranty, and that the Canadian user guide (`tandem-tslim-x2-ciq-user-guide-ca`, EN AW-1018762_B, FR AW-1019341_A) still names the Dexcom G6 and G7 (ruling C42). Tandem Mobi stays out until it is authorized in Canada.
6. MiniMed: Simplera Sync is now headlined as licensed by Health Canada. If it goes on sale, and a second registered page confirms it with the 780G, add it to both pickers with its basis.

## Sources named in this file

*Everything this file cites, with who publishes it and the passage each citation rests on. Please read the publisher column: it is where a manufacturer grant, a single province or a single hospital shows. "Locator" is the reviewer-only paraphrase kept in `sources-review.ts` — it is never rendered on a page, and it is what a claim in this file should be checked against.*

| `dc-air-travel` | Air Travel | Diabetes Canada | Canadian patient education | Paraphrase: insulin goes in carry-on, never checked; insulin keeps 30 days at room temperature; flying east and losing more than 2 hours may mean less intermediate or long-acting insulin; bring a doctor's letter. Ruled 2026-10-06 (C15): the 30 days here is not used, because some labels say 28. Also: temperature changes can damage insulin in checked luggage; do not wear a pump or CGM through the body scanner or put a pump through the X-ray, and ask for a physical search, in private if you wish; you need not disclose your diabetes or remove your pump, only tell the screening officer; a list of medicines from your pharmacist; spare supplies, an insulated bag in the heat and insulin close to the body in the cold. The insulin-unit changes for time zones are dosing and are not used anywhere on the site. | <https://www.diabetes.ca/living-with-diabetes/life-with-diabetes/the-rights-of-people-living-with-diabetes/air-travel> |
| `dq-all-about-injections` | All about injections | Diabète Québec | Canadian patient education | Paraphrase: 4–6 mm needles; rotate sites 1–2 cm apart; unopened insulin in the refrigerator (2 to 8 °C), never frozen or above 30 °C; opened insulin up to 28 days (42 for detemir). Re-read word for word by the Your Tools source check (2026-10-05): "Use short needles (4 mm, 5 mm or 6 mm) to avoid intramuscular injections"; in adults a skin lift should be used with a needle of 8 mm or longer, and may not be necessary with a 4 mm needle; a skin fold might be justified with a 5 or 6 mm needle where there is little fat; at least 1 to 2 cm (1 finger width) between sites, each area split into quadrants used a week each; regularly examine and palpate injection areas; avoid scars and beauty marks; injecting into a limb about to be exercised speeds the insulin and lowers blood glucose; check the vial or cartridge has not expired. The EN page says it is adapted from FIT 2015 (© January 2017, updated January 2019; reviewed by an RN), with 28 days in use (42 for detemir). The French page « Tout sur l’injection » (hrefFr, read 2026-10-06) is © Diabète Québec, January 2017, updated December 2025; it cites FIT Canada 4th ed. (2020) and is « Adapté de » a FIT PDF hosted by embecta (fit4diabetes.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/EMB-25-441-FIT-Recommendations-Update-Layout_F00-1.pdf); it gives in-use times of 28 days (42 for detemir and Toujeo, 56 for degludec), says a skin fold is « recommandé si on utilise une aiguille de 8 mm », and to avoid injecting within 2 to 3 cm of the navel. Ruled 2026-10-06 (C14): Diabète Québec is a Canadian non-industry patient organization that publishes and reviews these lines under its own name, so they stay live beside Diabetes Canada’s; lines whose only source is FIT stay held. Ruled 2026-10-06 (C15): "most are good for up to 28 days once opened, and some for longer" is cited to this page (Your Tools card 11, Staying Safe card 10). Reviewer evidence on in-use times from the Health Canada monographs (C7): Toujeo 42 days, Humalog 28, Tresiba 56, Awiqli 12 weeks, Entuzity 28. | <https://www.diabete.qc.ca/en/diabetes/diabetes-management/insulin/all-about-injections/> |
| `dc-cpg-ch9-monitoring-2021` | Blood Glucose Monitoring in Adults and Children with Diabetes: Update 2021 | Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines | Canadian guideline or position statement | Paraphrase: real-time CGM should be used in type 1 on injections or a pump, intermittently scanned CGM may be; rtCGM in type 1 pregnancy; time in range over 70% (3.9–10.0) and under 4% below 3.9 "for most individuals"; meter checks at least 3 times a day on insulin more than once daily; A1C about every 3 months, and at least every 6 months in adults who are stable at target. The time-in-range targets are the International Consensus Report’s, adopted here, and they exclude pregnancy, children and adolescents, and older or high-risk groups. Link this 2021 update, never the older chapter 9. | <https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-9-2021-update> |
| `dc-checking-blood-sugar` | Checking Blood Sugar | Diabetes Canada | Canadian patient education | Paraphrase: 4.0–7.0 before meals and 5.0–10.0 two hours after eating (5.0–8.0 if A1C is not at target); A1C ≤7.0%; explains meters and CGM. Re-read word for word by the Your Tools source check (2026-10-05): a finger prick puts blood on a test strip inserted into the monitor; monitors are available at most pharmacies or from your diabetes educator; get the proper training before you begin to use one; how often you check depends on your treatment plan; the "Ask your health-care provider about" list (how and where to draw blood, using and disposing of lancets, the size of the drop, the testing strips to use, cleaning the meter, checking its accuracy, coding it if needed); a CGM measures sugar in the fluid between cells; time in range is "the percentage of your day your blood sugar stays in your target range", given as 4.0–10.0 mmol/L for 70% or more of the day, with 3.9 or below for under 4%; individual targets may vary. Re-read 2026-10-06 for ruling C17, its section on being ill: check more often, such as every 2–4 hours; about 15 g of carbohydrate from drinks every hour if not eating; under "If you are sick and can’t eat…", call your doctor or go to the emergency room if you vomit or have diarrhea two or more times in 4 hours, and "If you use insulin, keep taking it when you are sick. Check with your health-care team about dose or medication changes." (both now on Staying Safe card 8). It also says "Keep taking your diabetes medications", which is not used: it conflicts with the Stay Safe sheet and CPG Ch15, which list medicines to pause on sick days. | <https://www.diabetes.ca/living-with-diabetes/blood-sugar-management/checking-blood-sugar> |
